benford_methodology_description: Why this test exists, what its results actually tell us, and when deviations should not mislead us.
benford_methodology_intro: Benford's law describes a surprising regularity: in many naturally-occurring datasets, the leading digit doesn't appear with equal frequency. The digit '1' shows up in about 30% of values, '2' in 18%, and '9' in only 4–5%. The phenomenon appears in city populations, river lengths, accounting ledgers — anywhere numbers span several orders of magnitude. Election forensics borrowed it on the hypothesis that fabricated results would struggle to follow the same curve. Reality is more complicated, and this page is devoted to those nuances.
benford_methodology_h_2bl: Why the test is for the second digit, not the first
benford_methodology_p_2bl1: The classical Benford test analyses the leading (first) digit. It applies when values vary considerably — for example single-digit numbers mixed with three- and four-digit ones. Per-section results don't behave that way. A standard Bulgarian polling station has 800–1000 registered voters. A party with 5–15% support collects votes that vary in a narrow range. That alone is enough for the first-digit test to 'fail' with no hint of manipulation anywhere.
benford_methodology_p_2bl2: Walter Mebane, one of the leading experts on the topic, demonstrates that the second digit is distributed much more uniformly and depends less on the magnitude of the number. The expected second-digit distribution (the '2BL' test) is nearly flat — '0' appears in about 12% of cases, '9' in about 8.5%. This method works on numbers that don't span several orders of magnitude. For that reason the site defaults to 2BL, while the classical first-digit test remains available via a toggle.
benford_methodology_p_thresholds1: We apply two main filters: a minimum number of votes for a party in a given section, and a minimum number of sections that pass that threshold. The second-digit test needs a number with at least two digits — under 10 votes there is simply no second digit to measure. Beyond that, the literature does not impose a high threshold for the votes per section, since the point of 2BL is precisely to work with smaller values. So our threshold is fixed at 10 votes per section, the same for both tests.
benford_methodology_p_thresholds2: Before any result is computed, we require at least 30 sections that pass the threshold. For smaller samples the chi-squared coefficient becomes unstable and MAD becomes too 'noisy'. Parties below this threshold are not displayed, to avoid misleading conclusions.
benford_methodology_h_metrics: How to read MAD and χ²
benford_methodology_p_metrics1: Two values appear under each chart:
benford_methodology_p_metrics_mad: MAD (mean absolute deviation): the average difference between the observed and Benford-expected shares. It does not depend on the number of sections, which makes it suitable for comparison across parties.
benford_methodology_p_metrics_chi: χ² (chi-squared): this value grows proportionally to n (the number of sections). Larger parties will have a higher χ² even if their distribution is identical to a smaller party's.
benford_methodology_p_metrics2: Based on the MAD value, we sort the results into three buckets:
benford_methodology_p_metrics_close: Close to Benford (MAD < 0.04) — the distribution tracks the curve within statistical noise.
benford_methodology_p_metrics_moderate: Moderate deviation (0.04 ≤ MAD < 0.08) — visible difference, often seen in parties whose result is concentrated in a narrow range.
benford_methodology_p_metrics_strong: Strong deviation (MAD ≥ 0.08) — pronounced difference, almost always driven by a specific scale of the data rather than misconduct.
benford_methodology_h_meaning: What the test shows and what it does NOT show
benford_methodology_p_meaning1: Strong deviation from Benford is almost never proof of manipulation. Most often it is an indication of a party with geographically concentrated support, or of results that cluster around specific values. In either case, 'clean' data can produce a bad Benford result.
benford_methodology_p_meaning2: The reverse holds too: a perfect Benford distribution is no certificate of honesty. Manipulation aimed at only a handful of sections, or one that scales the numbers by a constant factor, will not change the curve. Benford is a 'coarse filter' — useful for noticing that one party's data structurally differs from the rest, but not sufficient for final conclusions.
benford_methodology_h_alt: Where to look for real signals
benford_methodology_p_alt1: Three other tools on the site provide much more reliable signals than Benford:
benford_methodology_p_alt_risk: Risk screening: combines turnout outliers, unusual share concentration, machine-vs-paper divergence, and shifts during protocol re-entry.
benford_methodology_p_alt_problem: Problem sections: focuses on sections in higher-risk areas where one party's result departs sharply from the surrounding sections' average.
benford_methodology_p_alt_suspicious: Suspicious sections: sections with large gaps between machine and paper voting, or where final numbers differ substantially from the preliminary count.
benford_methodology_p_refs_mebane: Mebane, W. R. (2006). Election Forensics: Vote Counts and Benford's Law. Working paper, University of Michigan.
benford_methodology_p_refs_pericchi: Pericchi, L. & Torres, D. (2011). Quick Anomaly Detection by the Newcomb–Benford Law. Statistical Science, 26(4), 502–516.
benford_methodology_p_refs_klimek: Klimek, P., Yegorov, Y., Hanel, R. & Thurner, S. (2012). Statistical detection of systematic election irregularities. PNAS, 109(41), 16469–16473.
benford_methodology_p_refs_beber: Beber, B. & Scacco, A. (2012). What the Numbers Say: A Digit-Based Test for Election Fraud. Political Analysis, 20(2), 211–234.
benford_methodology_p_refs_nigrini: Nigrini, M. (2012). Benford's Law: Applications for Forensic Accounting, Auditing, and Fraud Detection. Wiley.
risk_methodology_description: How the risk score is computed: signals, weights, handling of missing data, categories, and how to interpret results.
risk_methodology_caveat_title: This is an analysis tool, not a verdict
risk_methodology_intro: This page describes the methodology for computing the risk score and — more importantly — what it cannot prove. The tool uses data we already publish in our individual reports. Combining them into a single index is a means of prioritizing review, not new evidence of wrongdoing.
risk_methodology_p_what1: Each polling section receives an index from 0 to 100 that summarizes how statistically atypical it is across seven independent criteria. The output is a ranked list of sections, prioritized for review.
risk_methodology_p_what2: It is not a fraud detector, nor a court-admissible irregularity indicator. The system cannot distinguish an administrative error from intentional action — every signal has its possible innocent explanations.
risk_methodology_p_signals_intro: Each signal is a normalized value (0 to 1) drawn from a specific per-section report. If section data for a particular report is missing, the signal stays "undefined" (not zero) and is handled via a special formula.
risk_methodology_signal_recount_p: Measures the magnitude of changes during the official recount: (added + removed votes) / total votes. Captures vote movement even when the net is zero. Normalized with a 10% cap — under a looser cap the signal was effectively inert.
risk_methodology_signal_suemg_p: Difference between the machine's flash-memory record (SUEMG) and the final protocol. Can be caused by technical errors during transfer or by recount adjustments not reflected in both records.
risk_methodology_signal_invalid_p: Share of paper ballots ruled invalid. Normalized with a 30% cap (values above that level are taken as 1.0). Caution: this signal is not demographically neutral — see the note on invalid ballots below.
risk_methodology_signal_additional_p: Share of voters added "under the line" on election day. Can be a sign of last-minute mobilization in small settlements, institutional voting, or coordinated pressure.
risk_methodology_signal_concentrated_p: Triggers when the winner in the section takes more than 80% of the vote. Below this threshold the signal is 0.
risk_methodology_signal_peer_p: Compares the section's turnout and winner share against neighboring sections in the same settlement (EKATTE). Captures sections that stand out sharply from their immediate surroundings.
risk_methodology_signal_swing_p: Compares the section's turnout and winner share against the same section at the previous election. Captures the "corporate vote" fingerprint — a section that previously split its vote now delivering a lopsided result at elevated turnout. Ratios are compared rather than absolute counts so the signal is robust to section renumbering. Only an upward shift relative to the national norm is flagged; a decline is not.
risk_methodology_p_formula1: The score is a weighted mean, not a simple sum. The denominator includes the weights of every signal that can be computed for the section:
risk_methodology_p_formula2: Where n_i is the value of the signal and w_i is its weight. The distinction between “computable” and “fired” matters: a signal that was checked and found nothing (no recount took place, for instance) enters at value 0 with its full weight. Only signals that cannot be computed at all leave the denominator — the machine comparison in a section with no machines, or the comparison against a prior election for the earliest vote. If a rare signal counted only when it fired, its mere presence would pull the section up the ranking.
risk_methodology_p_bands_intro: The number is a guide, but in the interface we use four main categories:
risk_methodology_band_low: No notable deviations. Most sections fall here.
risk_methodology_band_elevated: Some signals worth attention, but they can be coincidental.
risk_methodology_band_critical: Highly unusual data across multiple signals. A mandatory protocol review is recommended.
risk_methodology_important_percentile_p: Since high deviations are demographically normal in some municipalities (e.g. small mountain villages), the percentile helps determine whether a score is high only for that municipality or for the country as a whole.
risk_methodology_important_party_p: This column shows the section's winning party — same convention as every other per-section report. It is NOT the party "affected" by the risk. For specific information on which party gained or lost votes during a recount or flash-memory adjustment, see the per-section breakdown.
risk_methodology_important_evidence_p: A score of 85 based on 5 of 7 signals is much more reliable than the same score based on only 2 signals. Always check the count of available signals (e.g. 3/7).
risk_methodology_important_context_p: The badge for specific neighborhoods is informational only and does not affect the mathematical computation of risk. It helps the reader judge whether the demographic factor explains high concentration.
risk_methodology_p_how_to_use1: Start with the category, not the raw number. Check the count of available signals: scores backed by fewer than 3 signals are analysis-grade only and should not be used as evidence individually.
risk_methodology_p_how_to_use2: Open the per-section breakdown before quoting a score. The waterfall shows which signals fired and at what magnitude — without this context the number is meaningless. A score of 75 built from "all seven signals slightly elevated" is a very different story from a score of 75 built from "recount adjustment +35, everything else zero."
composite_methodology_description: How the composite index is computed — the five process-integrity signals that form the headline score, and the four context signals shown alongside.
composite_methodology_caveat_title: An analysis tool, not a verdict
composite_methodology_caveat_body: A high index value means an election is statistically unusual along several independent measures and deserves closer examination — nothing more. Each component can have a perfectly logical explanation, so always inspect the detailed breakdown before drawing conclusions.
composite_methodology_intro: The Election Risk Index is a 0–100 score that summarises five independent process-integrity signals. It sits at the top of the /risk-analysis page with the full breakdown, and in compact form on the home page under the Anomalies section. Alongside it we show four context signals (Benford, neighborhood swing, electoral volatility, polling error) that do NOT feed the headline — they can light up in perfectly clean elections.
composite_methodology_p_what1: The headline is the arithmetic mean of five process-integrity signals: section screening, machine integrity, missing flash, concentration, and procedural anomalies. Each is vote-weighted (as a share of national turnout, or of total machine votes for the machine-only signals) so it reads as "what fraction of the result this signal touches," not "how many places are flagged."
composite_methodology_p_what2: The formula applies only to available data. If older elections lack data (e.g. flash memory predates 2021), the index is computed from the remaining available process-integrity signals. Context signals are shown for every cycle where their data is available.
composite_methodology_p_what3: Splitting the signals into two tracks follows the international electoral-integrity frameworks (Pippa Norris PEI, V-Dem Election Quality Index, IFES). They do not mix process signals (audit-trail loss, protocol/flash disagreement) with context signals (statistical fingerprints, demographic volatility, forecast failure). Polling error in particular is NOT an irregularity signal — it is a prompt to inspect the process-integrity components more carefully.
composite_methodology_p_components_intro: Each component has a value from 0 to 100, and the links in the UI lead to the full source data for each. The headline is their simple average.
composite_methodology_c_sections_p: weighted share of national turnout sitting in sections with Elevated/High/Critical screening score (Critical weighted 1.0, High 0.5, Elevated 0.2). Calibrated cap — 5% of turnout = 100.
composite_methodology_c_machine_p: sum of absolute differences between flash memory and protocol per party, scaled to total machine votes. Calibrated cap — 0.2% drift = 100 (matching international audit-trigger thresholds).
composite_methodology_c_concentration_p: share of national turnout that went to the top party in settlements where it took ≥80% of valid votes. The classic signal of a controlled or 'captured' electorate. (Cap: 2% of turnout).
composite_methodology_c_procedural_p: combined share of national turnout from invalid ballots and additional voters in settlements where those rates exceed 10%. These two factors are often signs of organised or broker-driven voting. (Cap: 2% of turnout).
composite_methodology_p_context_intro: These signals are shown in a separate row and do NOT feed the headline average. They commonly light up in perfectly clean elections (new entrants, late deciders, range-bounded vote counts that fail Benford by construction).
composite_methodology_c_benford_p: share of parties (with over 100 sections) that show strong deviation (MAD ≥ 0.08) on the second-digit test. Benford on vote counts often fails by construction (Mebane 2006), which is why it is a context signal.
composite_methodology_c_polls_p: mean absolute error (MAE) of agencies for the cycle. A high value here signals forecast failure (new entrant, late deciders, legal blackout window), not an election irregularity. Excluded from the headline for that reason — but it should prompt a closer look at the process-integrity signals.
composite_methodology_c_clusters_p: share of the geolocatable elevated-risk sections that sit in a same-party geographic cluster — a knot of adjacent flagged sections won by one party. Calibrated on the 2005–2026 backtest (a stable 8–17% band): below 5% = 0, above 20% = 100. A context signal — it re-describes sections the section-screening component already counts, and clustering is partly a structural artefact of geographically correlated risk factors, so it is kept out of the headline.
composite_methodology_p_bands_intro: Bands are intentionally asymmetric, since the actual distribution in Bulgaria (2009–2026) shows that most 'clean' cycles fall in the 0–25 range.
composite_methodology_band_calm: No unusual signals on any component.
composite_methodology_band_elevated: At least one component shows mid-level deviation; typical for most post-2021 elections.
composite_methodology_band_high: Several components are simultaneously above mid-level; warrants careful analysis.
composite_methodology_band_critical: Many components are near their cap; extremely rare historically.
composite_methodology_important_caps_p: Component thresholds are calibrated to actually-observed data in 2009–2026, not to theoretical maxima.
composite_methodology_important_availabl: The headline uses all five process-integrity signals for elections from July 2021 onwards. For older cycles (before mass machine voting was introduced), 'Machine integrity' and 'Missing flash memory' are skipped and the index is computed from the remaining three. The comparison is fair but based on less information. Context signals are available only when their data exists for the cycle (neighborhood swing and electoral volatility require a prior cycle for comparison).
composite_methodology_important_polls_t: Why context signals are excluded from the headline:
composite_methodology_important_polls_p: Benford on vote counts often fails by construction (the test requires data spanning several orders of magnitude, but per-section party vote counts cluster in a narrow range). Polling error has structural causes unrelated to the electoral process (legal blackout, new entrants, late deciders). Electoral volatility measures political instability, not irregularity. Neighborhood swing is a cycle-on-cycle signal — substantive but threshold-sensitive. All four are shown, but outside the headline average.
composite_methodology_important_evidence: The index is a starting point for investigation, not a final piece of evidence. Always analyse which specific components form the final score.
risk_methodology_p_subscores: Alongside the composite we publish two separate sub-scores. The procedural sub-score (recount, machine comparison, invalid ballots, additional voters) is computed from the protocol paperwork and knows nothing about which party won the section. The distribution sub-score (concentration, deviation from neighbouring sections, shift against the prior vote) is computed from the vote distribution itself.
risk_methodology_p_subscores2: The distinction has a practical consequence. Any analysis of the form “party X's vote is concentrated in unusual sections” is circular against the distribution family, which already measures exactly that unusual concentration. For such questions use the procedural sub-score, not the composite.
risk_methodology_important_invalid_p: The procedural signals do not know which party won, but that does not make them demographically neutral. The share of invalid ballots is systematically higher in sections in Roma neighbourhoods — a documented pattern with plausible explanations such as literacy and ballot complexity, not necessarily manipulation. At municipality level this signal correlates with Roma population share (r = +0.36). A high value here should therefore not be read as evidence of irregularity, including within the procedural sub-score.
unit_cost_title: Cost per unit of service — methodology
unit_cost_description: How we compute the cost of one resolved court case, one kilometre of road and one hospital case — and what that number cannot tell you.
unit_cost_intro: In several places on this site we show the same kind of number: how much money goes into one unit of service delivered. Cost per resolved case, cost per kilometre, cost per hospital case. This page sets out the rules behind them once, so each tile does not have to explain itself.
unit_cost_p_what1: The number is cost per unit of SERVICE DELIVERED — money divided by units delivered. It is not an outcome. A "resolved case" does not mean a justly resolved case; a "hospital case" does not mean a cured patient; a kilometre of road does not mean a safe road.
unit_cost_p_what2: The distinction is not pedantic. Paying for outcomes ties money to measured change in people's lives. Cost per unit is a far more modest thing: what a unit of activity costs. We publish the second because the first does not exist in Bulgarian registers.
unit_cost_p_cannot1: Three limits apply to every tile in this family:
unit_cost_p_cannot_attribution: Attribution. The number does not separate the institution's contribution from everything else — legislative change, the economic cycle, demography. If cost per case rises, that may be inefficiency, or it may be harder cases.
unit_cost_p_cannot_quality: Quality. The denominator counts units, not what they were worth to the person. An institution that works faster and more superficially looks cheaper.
unit_cost_p_cannot_direction: Direction. A falling unit cost is not automatically good, nor a rising one automatically bad. An investment that raises the unit cost today and improves it tomorrow reads as deterioration.
unit_cost_p_cannot2: These numbers are therefore a position, not a verdict. They show where to look, not what happened.
unit_cost_p_law1a: Numerator and denominator must cover the same thing. The courts' budget is divided by the courts' cases — not the whole judiciary's budget by the courts' cases, which quietly folds tens of millions of euro of prosecution money into the cost of one court case.
unit_cost_p_law1b: This is the commonest mistake in such arithmetic and it is entirely invisible in the result: the number looks plausible, it is simply wrong by a constant factor.
unit_cost_p_law2a: When the units are not alike, a raw average means nothing. A hospital case can be dialysis at €25 or a transplant at €20,000. A hospital with an expensive profile looks wasteful and one with a light profile looks efficient, purely because of what it treats.
unit_cost_p_law2b: Comparison between institutions is therefore made against the EXPECTED cost for their own case mix, not against the overall average. Where no such adjustment is possible, no between-institution comparison is published.
unit_cost_p_legs: Each number is computed where its data lives, and carries its own scope:
unit_cost_leg_courts_basis: the courts' own appropriation divided by the cases they resolved; excludes the prosecution, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Supreme Administrative Court on both sides.
unit_cost_leg_roads_basis: contract value divided by the length of the section — only for contracts where the type of work and the parsed section allow a defensible figure.
unit_cost_p_notscore1: There is no cross-sector "efficiency index" and there will not be one. Cost per case, cost per kilometre and cost per hospital case are not commensurable; averaging them would manufacture a number corresponding to nothing.
unit_cost_p_notscore2: The family is a shared METHOD, not a shared scale.
unit_cost_p_health_context: Health has no such tile yet. Nationally the number is computable: the NHIF paid €2,247m for 3,835,420 reported cases in 2025, about €586 per case. But comparison BETWEEN hospitals requires a case-mix adjustment — precisely the second law above — and is therefore not published until that adjustment exists. The activity reports carry the procedure code without a price, i.e. volume, not value.
proc_meth_description: How each procurement risk flag is computed — the thresholds, the legal basis, when each check can be evaluated at all, and what the number does not tell you.
proc_meth_caveat_title: A flag is not a verdict
proc_meth_caveat_body: A fired flag means the behaviour is worth a second look — nothing more. It may be entirely lawful and unremarkable; it may be lawful but poor value for money; it may be illicit — in that order. We publish data, not verdicts: we are not an institution with a mandate to investigate.
proc_meth_intro: This page describes every flag, index and grade in our <dash>public-procurement</dash> module.
proc_meth_version_served: The flags being served were computed under flag set
proc_meth_version_drift: the code already declares a newer version; the cache has yet to be rebuilt.
proc_meth_p_abc: We follow the Open Contracting Partnership's framing: a fired flag may mean a) behaviour that is not at all illicit or suboptimal; b) not illicit, but suboptimal value for money; or c) illicit. That order is deliberate — the two innocent readings come first — and it is not a claim about which is more common.
proc_meth_p_denominator: The index's denominator is the number of checks that could actually be evaluated — never all of them. A contract with no recorded bid count is not scored zero on competition: the check is simply removed from its denominator. That is why the site shows a ratio ("2 of 9 checks"), not a bare number.
proc_meth_p_grades: A buyer's or supplier's grade is an availability-weighted mean: a component with no data is dropped from the denominator rather than scored zero. The one exception is the supplier's own political connection, which always counts. The two roles are weighted differently.
proc_meth_p_grades_differ: The supplier grade has no upheld-appeal component — a КЗК decision is a signal about the buyer's <tenders>procedure</tenders> — and it keeps the weights from before the 2026-07-18 rebalance. Whether that is a deliberate exception or an oversight is still open, and we assert neither.
proc_meth_shot_signals_alt: The fired-flags block on a contract page: the letter grade, the applicable-checks counter and the full ledger — the checks that fired, those that passed, and those that cannot be evaluated at all, each with its explanation and legal basis.
proc_meth_shot_signals_cap: An example from one contract page — awarded by the Road Infrastructure Agency to Avtomagistrali EAD. The ledger shows both the checks that passed and the ones that could not be evaluated, with the reason why.
proc_meth_shot_grades_alt: Two grade cards for the same entity — 'as a buyer' and 'as a supplier' — each with a letter, a score out of 100 and a bar per component.
proc_meth_shot_grades_cap: An example: one entity in both roles (Avtomagistrali EAD). The grades differ because they are computed over different components and with different weights — not because one refutes the other.
proc_meth_p_align: Every check is positioned against its closest indicator in <ocp>OCP's Red Flags for Integrity (2024)</ocp> and in <im>iMonitor 2.0</im>, based on the documents themselves rather than a summary of them.
proc_meth_p_align_unmapped: {{unmapped}} of the checks have no OCP equivalent — among them the two political-connection checks, the part of this set that is most specific to Bulgaria.
proc_meth_limit_validation: Decarolis & Giorgiantonio (2022) checked the most-scrutinised red flags against police-investigation data covering a near-complete set of Italian roadwork contracts, and found them either uncorrelated with corruption or negatively associated with it. That is the strongest argument against reading any single flag as evidence.
proc_meth_limit_goodhart: A published flag is also a specification for evading it. We publish anyway, and deliberately: flags fire for review, and grades are measured at entity level, where a pattern is harder to stage than a single contract.
proc_meth_limit_construct: The flags measure procedural characteristics associated with weak competition and discretion. They do not measure corruption, and no threshold here is a probability of wrongdoing.
proc_meth_p_reuse: The catalogue and the handbook are MIT-licensed. Cite the version shown above — it describes the flags that were actually served, not the version in the code.
proc_meth_dl_json: the machine-readable catalogue (the same source the handbook is generated from)
proc_meth_comp_connectedSelf: the company is itself politically connected
proc_meth_avail_conditional: only where the data exists (otherwise dropped from the denominator)
proc_meth_p_tender: These score the <tenders>procedure</tenders> itself, so a signal can fire while bids are still open, and they say something about the buyer's conduct rather than about any winner. Unlike the contract-level checks, these are not precomputed or stored: they are recalculated from the procedure row each time you open the page. So they always follow the latest rules without waiting for a rebuild — but they are also never weighted into an A–F grade.
proc_meth_p_contract_grade: The letter beside a single contract is banded on the number of checks that fired, not on the ratio. This is deliberate, and measured: on the entity-grade scale the ratio would put 99% of the corpus in A or B and make F mathematically unreachable, because the highest ratio in the corpus is 60. A means nothing fired; F means five or more. A single contract is one observation — its letter is weaker evidence than an entity's, and should be read that way.
